metadata.name: Acute laryngitis
metadata.emergency_level: Routine - but airway compromise (esp. children/epiglottitis) is an emergency
metadata.severity: Usually mild and self-limiting; persistent hoarseness needs assessment

overview.short_description: Inflammation of the larynx causing hoarseness or voice loss, usually viral and self-limiting, that resolves within about two weeks with voice rest and supportive care.
overview.detailed_description: Acute laryngitis is common, usually part of a viral upper respiratory infection or from voice overuse. It is self-limiting. The important task in primary care is to reassure and advise, and to recognise persistent hoarseness (>3 weeks), which requires assessment (laryngoscopy) to exclude laryngeal cancer, especially in smokers, and to recognise airway red flags (stridor, drooling) suggesting more serious pathology.
overview.pathophysiology: Viral infection or mechanical/chemical irritation inflames the vocal cords, impairing their vibration and producing hoarseness or aphonia.
overview.etiology: Usually viral (as part of a URTI); also voice overuse, smoking, gastro-oesophageal reflux (laryngopharyngeal reflux), irritants/allergens; bacterial causes are less common.
overview.natural_history: Hoarseness typically resolves within 1-2 weeks; persistent (>3 weeks) hoarseness needs investigation.
overview.prognosis: Excellent for acute viral laryngitis; the concern is missing persistent hoarseness due to malignancy.

mortality.value: Negligible (except via missed serious causes of hoarseness).

epidemiology.age_groups: All ages; croup (viral laryngotracheitis) affects young children specifically.

risk_factors.smoking: Irritant; major risk factor for chronic laryngitis and laryngeal cancer.
risk_factors.alcohol: Irritant; with smoking increases laryngeal cancer risk.
risk_factors.obesity: Associated with reflux, which can cause laryngitis.
risk_factors.occupation: Heavy voice use; exposure to fumes/dust.
risk_factors.medications: Inhaled corticosteroids (without spacer/rinsing) can cause hoarseness/candidiasis.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Gastro-oesophageal/laryngopharyngeal reflux; allergic rhinitis; recurrent URTIs.

chief_complaints.complaint: Hoarse voice or loss of voice

symptoms.importance: RED FLAG - airway emergency (not simple laryngitis)

negative_findings.why_important: Not typical of simple acute laryngitis - mandates laryngoscopy to exclude laryngeal cancer (especially smokers)

negative_findings.finding: No stridor, drooling, or breathing difficulty
negative_findings.why_important: Absence argues against airway emergencies (epiglottitis, croup severity)

history_questions.question: How long has the hoarseness lasted?
Do you smoke or drink alcohol heavily?
history_questions.why_ask: Major risk factors for laryngeal cancer

history_questions.question: Any breathing difficulty, noisy breathing, drooling, or severe pain?
Reflux symptoms, heavy voice use, or inhaled steroid use?
Any neck lump, difficulty swallowing, or unintentional weight loss?

physical_examination.examination: General ENT/throat exam and voice assessment
physical_examination.expected_finding: Hoarse voice; oropharynx often normal or mild URTI signs
Should be normal; a neck mass is a red flag

physical_examination.examination: Airway assessment (stridor, work of breathing) especially in children
Chest exam if lower respiratory symptoms

imaging.when_needed: Persistent hoarseness or suspected malignancy (ENT-directed imaging after laryngoscopy)

other_diagnostic_tests.endoscopy: Laryngoscopy (flexible) by ENT is the key investigation for persistent hoarseness to visualise the vocal cords
other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Biopsy of any suspicious laryngeal lesion

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical: acute hoarseness/dysphonia (usually <3 weeks) in the context of a URTI or voice strain, without airway compromise or red-flag features. Persistent hoarseness (>=3 weeks) is NOT diagnosed as simple laryngitis without laryngoscopy.

cutoff_values.value: Hoarseness lasting >=3 weeks (especially in smokers/>=45) warrants urgent suspected-cancer referral for laryngoscopy (NICE NG12).

differential_diagnosis.differences: Persistent (>3 weeks), smoker/drinker, neck lump, dysphagia, weight loss
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_exam: Vocal cord lesion on laryngoscopy; neck node
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Has the hoarseness lasted more than 3 weeks, and do you smoke?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Toxic, severe odynophagia, drooling, stridor, muffled voice
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any drooling, noisy breathing, or difficulty breathing?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Barking cough, inspiratory stridor, young child
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is this a young child with a barking cough and noisy breathing?
Is it chronic/recurrent with reflux or heavy voice use?

diagnostic_questions.question: How long has the hoarseness lasted, and do you smoke?
diagnostic_questions.purpose: Do not miss persistent hoarseness needing laryngoscopy

diagnostic_questions.question: Any noisy breathing, drooling, or difficulty breathing?

next_best_question.current_situation: Hoarseness with a cold, no airway red flags
next_best_question.question: How long has it lasted, do you smoke, and any breathing difficulty or neck lump?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Acute (<3 weeks), well -> voice rest + supportive advice; >=3 weeks or smoker/neck lump -> urgent ENT (laryngoscopy); airway red flags -> emergency

next_best_test.why: Persistent hoarseness (>=3 weeks) or red flags

red_flags.finding: Stridor, drooling, or difficulty breathing (especially in children)
red_flags.immediate_action: Airway emergency - urgent ENT/paediatric assessment; do not distress a child or examine the throat

red_flags.finding: Hoarseness persisting >=3 weeks, especially in a smoker/drinker or age >=45
Neck lump, difficulty swallowing, or unintentional weight loss
Haemoptysis or persistent throat pain with referred ear pain

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Persistent hoarseness (>=3 weeks) or other head/neck cancer red flags - urgent ENT/laryngoscopy.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Recurrent/chronic hoarseness (reflux, nodules, voice misuse) for ENT/speech therapy.

early: Airway compromise (in epiglottitis/severe croup - not simple laryngitis)
late: Missed laryngeal malignancy if persistent hoarseness not investigated

initial_management.supportive_care: Reassurance that acute laryngitis is self-limiting; voice rest (avoid whispering, which strains cords); hydration; steam/humidification; analgesia.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: AAOHNS_DYSPHONIA_2018.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Rest the voice, stop smoking, avoid irritants and alcohol, stay hydrated, manage reflux.
initial_management.follow_up: Return if hoarseness persists beyond 3 weeks (needs ENT) or airway symptoms develop.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Symptomatic only (analgesia); antibiotics are NOT indicated for viral laryngitis. Treat contributory reflux (lifestyle +/- acid suppression) or optimise inhaled-steroid technique if relevant.

patient_education.home_advice: Laryngitis is usually a viral inflammation of the voice box that clears within a couple of weeks. Rest your voice (don't whisper), drink fluids, breathe steam, and avoid smoking. Antibiotics don't help. Importantly, see a doctor if your hoarse voice lasts more than three weeks (especially if you smoke), or if you develop a neck lump, trouble swallowing, or difficulty breathing.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: التهاب الحنجرة غالباً التهاب فيروسي في صندوق الصوت يزول خلال أسبوعين تقريباً. أرِح صوتك (لا تهمس)، واشرب السوائل، واستنشق البخار، وتجنّب التدخين. المضادات الحيوية لا تفيد. والمهم: راجع الطبيب إذا استمرّت البُحّة أكثر من ثلاثة أسابيع (خاصةً إن كنت مدخّناً)، أو ظهرت كتلة في الرقبة، أو صعوبة بلع، أو صعوبة تنفّس.
patient_education.prevention: Avoid voice strain and smoking; stay hydrated; manage reflux.
patient_education.warning_signs: Hoarseness lasting more than three weeks, a neck lump, difficulty swallowing or breathing, noisy breathing/drooling (especially in children), or coughing up blood.

prevention.vaccination: Not specific (influenza vaccination reduces some URTIs).
prevention.lifestyle: Voice care, smoking cessation, hydration, reflux management.

evidence.evidence_level: High for self-limiting course and against antibiotics; strong for investigating persistent hoarseness.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by AAOHNS_DYSPHONIA_2018; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong - NICE (NG12 for persistent hoarseness), AAO-HNS hoarseness guideline.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Support voice recovery and identify serious or persistent causes of dysphonia.
treatment_guidance.legacy_narrative_summary: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: AAOHNS_DYSPHONIA_2018.
required_history_before_any_medication: age and weight where dosing is weight- or age-dependent
pregnancy or breastfeeding status when relevant
documented drug allergies and the exact reaction
all prescribed, OTC, herbal and recreational substances
major cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and bleeding history
non_drug_measures: Voice conservation (not forceful whispering), hydration, smoking avoidance; do not routinely use antibiotics, corticosteroids or antireflux drugs without a specific indication.

medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: severe active liver disease or prior serious reaction
use_caution_if: heavy alcohol use, malnutrition, low body weight, or concomitant paracetamol-containing products
monitoring: total daily exposure and clinical response

medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: active gastrointestinal bleeding/ulcer, serious NSAID allergy, or NSAID-triggered asthma
use_caution_if: chronic kidney disease, heart failure, hypertension, anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy, older age, pregnancy, or dehydration
monitoring: renal function, blood pressure, oedema and gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms when clinically indicated

procedures_referral_and_escalation: Immediate airway assessment for stridor/respiratory distress; laryngeal examination for persistent dysphonia or sooner with cancer/neurological risk.
